title: AI agents become the default for knowledge work
summary: Software, finance, law and research move to agent-first workflows: a human sets the goal and reviews, an agent does the work.
detail: The shift is already underway in software engineering and is spreading to any job whose output is a document, a decision or a model. The tell is not that agents exist but that firms reorganize around them: headcount plans assume agents, procurement buys agent seats, and junior roles are redefined as agent supervision. By the end of 2027 a majority of large firms in these four sectors run most routine knowledge work through agents.

title: The first US presidential election fought substantially over AI
summary: Labor displacement, compute control and accountability dominate the campaign.
detail: AI will not be the only issue, but it will be the organizing one: who is responsible when an agent causes harm, whether compute is national infrastructure, what the state owes workers displaced by systems it licensed. title: The hinge resolves: pluralism or concentration
summary: Either capability stays contested across many actors (57%), or one or two actors consolidate a decisive lead (43%).
detail: Everything after this point branches. In the pluralism branch, open models stay close to the frontier, compute is spread across many actors, and governance is negotiated among rivals. It is chaotic and dangerous and broadly free. In the concentration branch, one firm or state closes the research loop first and compounds its lead until nobody can catch up. That branch produces the century's best outcomes if the leader is benevolent and competent, and its worst if not. The forecast puts 57% on pluralism, mostly because concentration requires sustained secrecy and no serious mistakes. A third shape appeared in 2026 and is scored as concentration-leaning: a government-gated frontier of three to five labs that pace each other by agreement, with open weights a year or more behind.

title: Autonomous weapons kill at scale in a war between states
summary: Munitions that pick their own target and strike with no human approving that target, documented in the thousands. The first kills are already on record; what is missing is the count.
detail: The capability arrived before the rules. On 6 July 2026 a Russian Molniya drone with an Nvidia Jetson Orin board and no radio antenna chose propane tanks at a Zaporizhzhia filling station and killed three civilians; Ukrainian forensics read the unencrypted targeting code (New York Times, 24 August 2026). CSIS's June 2026 brief says Russia is already fielding fully autonomous systems and that drones fly roughly 80% of strike missions on both sides. Ukraine's Brave1 says successful strikes with AI auto-homing rose tenfold in the first eight months of 2026, and a defence-ministry adviser wrote that navigation, target search and attack 'will be fully autonomous'. On 25 August 2026 the UN Secretary-General and the ICRC president said the world is 'dangerously close' to autonomous targeting of humans, 'amid unconfirmed reports' it is already happening. The 2025 UN resolution passed 164 to 6; the US, Russia and Israel voted no, and NSPM-11 (5 June 2026) ordered the Pentagon to rewrite Directive 3000.09 within 90 days to remove barriers to fielding. The bet is that by the end of 2028 someone credible counts it: a belligerent, a UN monitoring mission, the ICRC or SIPRI documents thousands of engagements in which the machine, not a person, selected the target. Terminal homing on a target a human picked does not count; a human choosing an area and the munition choosing what to hit inside it does.

title: A Taiwan Strait blockade or war cuts off leading-edge chips for 90 days

detail: In the third quarter of 2026, 41% of TSMC's wafer revenue came from 3nm and 2nm, nodes made nowhere else; 79% came from 7nm and below. Arizona's second fab reaches volume in the third quarter of 2027 (3nm) and Japan's second fab in 2028 (3nm), and TrendForce has Taiwan's share of advanced-node capacity falling from 71% in 2021 to 58% in 2030, so the exposure shrinks through the window but never goes away. The PLA has run a named blockade rehearsal around the island every year since 2022; Justice Mission-2025 (29-31 December) put rockets inside Taiwan's contiguous zone and drilled 'integrated blockade and control' with 28 navy and coast-guard ships. Taiwan holds under two months of coal and gas, so a full blockade stops the fabs through the grid before it stops the ships. Against that: CSIS's 26 wargames found a blockade 'a serious gamble' that does not guarantee success, experts polled by CSIS in December 2025 named the South China Sea, not the Strait, as 2026's likeliest flashpoint, and no large named exercise had been held in 2026 as of mid-October. The 1996 missile crisis interrupted shipping for days, not months. A seven-year window at a hazard of two to three percent a year gives 13-20%; the 90-day bar and the fact that chips move by air cut the quarantine scenarios out. Fifteen percent. The midterm reading is the one to watch: the leaders' detente excludes chips, and 68% of CSIS's experts think Beijing now sees Washington as less committed to Taiwan.

title: The nuclear taboo holds
summary: No nuclear weapon detonated in anger through 2060. The forecast puts 68% on the taboo holding, which is a 32% chance that one is used in the next 34 years.
detail: Eighty-one years without a weapon used in war is the base rate, and a naive reading of it gives about a 29% chance of use in the next 34 years. The 2026 picture argues for a little worse than that. New START expired on 5 February 2026 and for the first time since 1972 no treaty caps the two largest arsenals; Russia says it observes the old limits only as long as the US does, and on 20 October 2026 its deputy foreign minister said there were 'no grounds' for strategic stability talks. SIPRI counts 12,187 warheads in January 2026, 4,012 deployed and 2,100 to 2,200 on high alert; the stockpiles of China, India, Pakistan and North Korea are growing, and the Pentagon expects China's to reach 1,000 by 2030. Three nuclear-armed states fought in 2025-26: Russia in Ukraine, India against Pakistan, and the US and Israel against Iran in a war that began on 28 February 2026, has not formally ended, and has Iranian officials asking aloud whether to stay in the NPT. The Bulletin set the Clock to 85 seconds on 27 January 2026, its closest ever. The line is written as the null, as the-silence is: the claim is that the taboo holds, and the number is the chance it does. A single detonation counts against it, however small.

title: The AI trade halves
summary: The chip index that carries the AI boom closes 50% below its record. It has done that twice before, in 2000-02 and 2008, each time after a capex cycle outran the cash to pay for it. About even odds it happens between 2027 and 2030.
detail: The five big hyperscalers will spend more than $690 billion on capex in fiscal 2026, up over 80% in a year, with free cash flow near zero or negative at three of the five and new debt covering 32% of capex, up from 9% in 2024 (FactSet, July 2026). title: AI shows up in the productivity statistics
summary: Solow's line again: AI is everywhere but in the numbers. The test is three straight years of US labor productivity growth above 2.5%, a run last seen in 1998-2004, with the third year landing between 2032 and 2036.
detail: BLS private nonfarm business labor productivity grew 2.3% in 2023, 3.0% in 2024 and 2.2% in 2025; total factor productivity slowed to 0.8% in 2025. title: Another pandemic kills a million, confirmed
summary: COVID-19 has 7.1 million confirmed deaths on WHO's count. The bet is a new outbreak that passes one million confirmed deaths before 2051: about 40%, roughly what the historical record says, nudged up for spillover and down for vaccines.
detail: The base rate is not small. Marani and colleagues (PNAS 2021), fitting 400 years of epidemic records, put the recurrence time of a COVID-intensity pandemic at about 129 years and the lifetime chance of living through one at 38%, with the rate rising as spillover rises; Airfinity's 2023 model gave 27.5% in ten years for a pandemic as deadly as COVID, falling to 8% if vaccines arrive within 100 days. Spread over 2027-2050 those rates give anywhere from a one-in-six to a better-than-even chance. The bar here is lower than COVID: one million confirmed deaths is a seventh of COVID's count, roughly a 1957- or 1968-flu-sized event reported with modern surveillance. The watch list is unchanged. H5N1 has infected 1,022 people since 1997 with 12 cases and 3 deaths worldwide from August 2025 to June 2026, no person-to-person spread, and WHO's risk to the public 'remains low'. The institutions are half-built: the WHO Pandemic Agreement was adopted in May 2025, but its pathogen-sharing annex missed the May 2026 Assembly and is now due by May 2027, and the Agreement cannot open for signature until the annex is done. Origin does not matter for this line; an engineered pathogen that clears the bar also resolves mass-casualty-event.

title: A quarter of American adults are on a GLP-1

title: The first ice-free Arctic September
summary: A September monthly mean below 1 million km² of sea ice, the standard 'ice-free' threshold. 2026's minimum was 4.60 million km²; the models say the first crossing is likely before 2050, the data say the decline has stalled for two decades.

The window is 2036–2050 with the odds centred in the mid-2040s. A first ice-free day (Heuzé and Jahn, 2024: possible within three to six years of 2023 conditions in the fastest models) would come first and does not count.

title: Political ads must prove where their pictures came from
summary: A binding US federal rule that political ads disclose AI-made content, or a US or EU rule that political-ad media carry signed provenance credentials. The EU labels ads and marks AI output already; nobody yet requires the ad itself to carry its origin.
detail: The pieces exist and do not join up. The EU's political-advertising regulation (2024/900) has applied since 10 October 2025 and requires a label saying who paid, how much and who was targeted; Meta and Google stopped selling political ads in the EU rather than comply. The AI Act's Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026: providers must mark generative output in a machine-readable way (existing systems have until 2 December 2026) and deployers must label deepfakes, with a Commission code of practice (June 2026) specifying signed metadata plus watermarking. Neither says a political ad's footage must carry a credential. In the US the FCC proposed on-air AI disclosure for broadcast political ads in July 2024 (MB Docket 24-211); Republican commissioners opposed it, a Senate bill was filed to forbid it, and it has not moved. The FEC voted 5–1 in September 2024 to apply existing fraud rules instead of writing AI ones. The states filled the gap: NCSL counted 31 with election-deepfake laws by June 2026, 28 of them disclosure laws, and California's FPPC is writing the regulation for its AB 2355 ad-disclosure statute. The courts are the headwind: California's AB 2655 was struck in August 2025 and a federal judge blocked Montana's law in September 2026. The bet is that a 2028-cycle deepfake incident, or an EU Democracy Shield review of the TTPA, turns labels into required provenance.

title: Africa's working-age population passes China and India combined
summary: The UN's 2024 medium projection has Africans aged 15–64 overtaking China and India together in 2058, 1,773 million to 1,744 million, the same year Africa passes every other UN region. Most of those workers are already born.
detail: In 2024 Africa had 867 million people aged 15–64 against 1,974 million in China and India. The UN's 2024 medium variant has Africa at 1,559 million by 2050 and 1,825 million by 2060 while China falls below 900 million in 2038 and India's working-age population peaks in 2048 at 1,135 million; the lines cross in 2058. The same year Africa passes Central and Southern Asia, the largest of the UN's SDG regions, so the two natural framings of the line agree. Africa's share of the world's working-age population goes from 16% to 29% by 2060 and 41% by 2100; between 2024 and 2060 Africa adds more working-age people than the world does, because everywhere else is shrinking. The demography is firm because everyone who will be 15–64 in 2058 is born by 2043, and China's decline is already in the pyramid. What can move the year is African fertility falling faster than the UN assumes, which recent revisions have tended to find, so the window runs four years either side of the UN's date. Whether the dividend is collected is the story of the second half of the century; this line only grades the arithmetic.
